title: SWE-Prime: 10% of the Trajectories, Better Results
hook: A successful agent trajectory can still be full of wasted and risky steps. Filter down to the best 10% and fine-tuning beats training on everything that worked.
key_points: Task success does not guarantee good supervision — successful trajectories still contain ineffective, redundant, or risky steps.
Training on them teaches the model to imitate undesirable problem-solving behavior.
Stage 1 screens whole trajectories on process quality, result quality, and representativeness.
Stage 2 groups consecutive steps into semantic segments and scores each on contribution, learnability, and risk.
All segments stay in the sequence to preserve context; only selected segments contribute to the loss.
Training on the selected 10% subset beats training on the full resolved dataset — up to 12.2% relative gain on SWE-Bench Pro and 24.2% on SWE-Bench Verified.
content_html: The recipe for training coding agents has been: run a lot of trajectories, keep the ones that resolved the issue, fine-tune on those. Zheng and colleagues point out the flaw. Success is an outcome signal, and a trajectory that reached the right patch may have flailed to get there — dead ends, redundant edits, risky commands. SFT does not distinguish; it imitates all of it.
extra_html:
The method

SWE-Prime filters in two granularities. Trajectory level screens whole runs on process quality, result quality, and data representativeness, producing a high-quality and still-representative subset of successful trajectories. Segment level then groups consecutive steps into semantic segments and scores each on its contribution to the final solution, its learnability, and its potential risk.

The implementation detail that makes this work: during SFT, all segments remain in the sequence so context is preserved, but only selected segments contribute to the loss. You cannot delete a bad step without breaking the story of the ones that follow — so you keep it visible and refuse to learn from it.

Results

Training on the 10% trajectory subset that SWE-Prime selects outperforms training on the full resolved dataset, with relative gains of up to 12.2% on SWE-Bench Pro and 24.2% on SWE-Bench Verified.

The general lesson applies well beyond code: when your supervision comes from a verifier, the verifier tells you the answer was right, not that the reasoning was worth copying.

related.title: PILOT: Self-Improvement While the Run Is Still Going
related.hook: Most agent self-improvement happens after the run ends, too late to save it. PILOT gives a supervisor the power to redirect or abort a live worker — and cuts output tokens by nearly half.

related.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real GitHub Issues?
related.hook: Test a coding agent on real GitHub issues with real test suites - not toy problems - and the bar turns out to be much harder than HumanEval suggested.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'the task succeeded' a weak filter for training data?
flashcards.back_html: Success is an outcome, not a process judgment. A trajectory can reach the right answer through redundant, ineffective, or risky steps — and SFT will happily teach all of them.

flashcards.prompt: Why does SWE-Prime keep unselected segments in the sequence?

choices.text: To preserve context, while excluding them from the loss computation
Because removing them would break tokenization
To let the model learn from them with a lower learning rate

flashcards.explanation_html: Later steps only make sense given earlier ones, so the text must stay visible. Masking the loss is how you avoid imitating a step without deleting its context.

flashcards.prompt: What are the three criteria for segment-level selection?
flashcards.back_html: A segment's contribution to the final solution, its learnability, and its potential risk.
